THE COLONIAL TRADE OF FRANCE. The present position oh the French Colonies, in reference to the ch.nges which arc being introduced into the Commercial policy of France, is a subject which, us that policy expands and developes, assumes the greatest importance, and I cannot fail to uffod matter for earnest consideration to the Emperor and his advisers. An Imperial decree has recently appeared, repealing Colonies n a principal article of Colonial the additional tax on foreign sugar, and thus lemoving the piotection enjoyed hy the French . produce. This step in advance is one which cannot be taken alone, otherwise it will inflict gioss huidship oil the plainer, who will be sacrificed for the ben. fit of the consumer iu the mother country. It is clear, thcrefoie, that the Custom-house sysnm which still exists between France and her Colonies, is doomed, and that, all restrictions upon the employment of foreign tonnage lor the transport of Colonial produce into France, and of the products ol France into h< r d pend tides, must also lie letunv. d, and the Carrying Trad, so tar r. ndeied absolutely free. The þÿ compact between France and her t domes, as i' h >s beeu termed, dates from the time ol Louis XIV., and is, iib it has been justly observed by n writer in the Debats , on the point of expiring. Under that arrangement France

reserved for herself þÿ all the produce deemed u.-elul for her consumption and for her foreign Commerce, particularly sugar, coffee, cotton, cocoa, and tobacco. She imposed on the Coloni-ts the exclusive use of her natural or manufactured productions, prohibiting, under pain of the galleys, any Commerce with a foreign country. Navigation was possessed as a monopoly hy the national flag, and this principle lias received during a century an aggravation which Colbeit had not foreseen þÿ the Colonies, without special exception, could not traffic one with the other It was thus that the blue cloths of Pondicherry were obliged to he brought to France, in order to he admitted into Senegal, which, nevertheless, lay in th. ir road; and when Martinique wi.-hed to get coffee Imm her sister island, Cuadaloupc, only a þÿday sail s distant, she was oblig'd to have it fiom þÿFiance. The system, it is obvious, has been maintained at the expense of those possessions whieh it is the special object of the present regime to forster and enlarge; hut it is also utteily inconsistent with the policy of the Emperor, and cannot continue to eo-exist with it. The French Colonists are themselves conscious of the position in which the Heine Government is placed in reference to free imp.iris, and they are also conscious of i he ir ow'n rights. Our readers have s. en that the people of Martinique and Guadeloupe have boldly addressed the Empe-or, and asked for a. liberation of that Trade on which their pros-

perity, if not their very existence, may be said to depend, and the appeal has not been made ii» vain. The Imperial Government has decretd within the past year the removal of duty on articles of food imported into the Colonies in question, and the importation of machinery on the same conditions as into France. To these advantages m .v he added the establishment of" a Discount B .nk, and the mention of a C denial (Ji edit Company, from which institutions the Colonists have already reaped veiy decided advantages. þÿ In order to complete and strengthen these advantages (observes the Debuts ) the Colonies call lor what France herself adopts to promote her own prospetity þÿ a better economical regime. The reform, in order to he develop, d with safety, ought to be accomplished in the name of a piinciple of public light too long misunderstood. The Colonics are French, and not foreign countries; they are, in a manner, simple provinces which revolutions of the globe have detached from the continental teirilory of Fiance and dispersed across the sea. B. tween the Colonies and the mother courtry, and between one Colony and another, the Customhouses me internal ones, condemned hy the same principle of national unity which in the year 1790 only served to overthrow the fiscal burners which separated the provinces. Thus, between the diffuietit parts of the Empire the circulation of merchandise of Colonial production ought to be as free as h. tween the French departments, and their rights to importation, exportation, and

flag ught to lie the same, with some few well- (, jusiified exceptions. þÿ Such, then, are the concessions claimed for the French Colonies, on the ground- of common souse and common justice. They cannot be refund by tl.e Fiencli Government without 8'ultifying the Commercial policy which has been di fiuitively adopted by the present Ruhr of Franco, and whieh, if we are rightly informed, lie is not only piepared, but detei mined, to carry to its legitimate conclusion. The French Colonial system, which m> ant the sacrifice of the inteiests of the Colonists to those of the producers ill the mother country, is thus virtually at an end The exclusiveness which has doomed for 150 ycats Ihe most valuable possessions of France to improgre-sion and inactivity, is about to be exchange I for tree intercourse, and for (hot encouragement which Trade always derives from the application of a low tariff. But if the French Colonial Trade is to be tree, so must be her Navigation. 100,000 tons of Shipping will never suffice to carry the expanding Commerceof Martinique and Guadeloupe, of Reunion and Pondicherry, to its destination in Europe or elsewhere. The abolition or r.duction ol the Colonial import duiies means also the immediate opening of the Colonial Carrying Trade, or it means nothiug at all. Our readers will no doubt recollect the contents of the Royal Ordinance of 24th April 1860, concerning the future publicity of the Colonial Council's meetings. The Ordinance enacts that the meetings shall be public, the accession to tliern, during the debates of the Council, to he dependent on such conditions, as the Council, with the sanction of the Governor, may lix for maintaining order; and t hat the Governor shall be entitled to demand that any subject be discussed within closed doors; and the Council has the right to resolve on the same .course of proceeding in such manner as may be accurately defined in its regulations. With regard to the opening of the fifth session of the Colonial Council, which will take place to-morrow, v\e have, however, been informed, that this can not be public, as it is requisite, that the Assembly should first have constituted itself, elected a chairman, and then adopt such additions to the

regulations by which the conditions for the publicity of the meetings are to be decided. We venture to hope that the members of the Council will give as wide an interpretation to the limits of this ordinance as possible. The regulation regarding the exclusion of the public in certain cases, where the order of the meeting may he disturbed, is one adopted by the most liberal representative institutions; yet it is one seldom or never put in force ; and whenever done, it is applied to the general public, an exception being made to the reporters lor the Press. We recommend l his circumstance to the consideration of the Council, for in those cases where the public here may be excluded from the dehates, it is then that the Press can he of most use in giving some information of whatever transpired during that exclusion ; a circumstance that will not fail to satisfy the public that, the exclusion was only a matter of necessity in order that the Council should be unrestrained in the debating of some particular subject.

The Fearful Earthquakes m South America þÿ The U tters by tbe Brazil mail, delivered on Tuesday, bring deplorable accounts of the loss ol life and property which has been occasioned by the fearful earthquake in South America. It was generally imagined that the statemeut in the telegrams that 7,000 persons had perished in tbe town of Mcudoza, iu the Argentine Republic, was an exaggeration, but the accounts now to hand show that the extent of the calamity at that point has not been overstated, and give

forward from oilier quartern. It would appear tliat this earthquake was inferior in violence to none recorded in history. The private letters state that " the city of Mcndoza is no more,'' and the number of persons who have perished there is variously computed at from 6,100 to 7,000. The loss of lite was probably rendered the greater by tile circumstance that the cmtliquake was preceded by a remarkable stoi m and by a but rain, which drove the inhabitants into their dwellings for shelter. The Governor escaped. Already a disaster, only inferior in importance, is aunouueed from another town, the gieuter part of San Juan having been destroyed, and 3,000 persons being reported to have been killed. San Juan is situated 120 leagues to the north of Mendoza, at the foot of the Andes. The shock was felt with such severity at. Cordova, 150 leagues from Meudozu, that the church was thrown down. It was also felt on the same day (the 20th of March) and hour, but without any serious effects at Buenos Ay res. As the earthquake appears to have eome down from the di'ection of Valparaiso, or its neighbourhood, considerable anxiety is felt for the receipt of further accounts from that quarter, the news by the present opportunity extending only to the 15th of March, when attention was chiefly directed to the great mercantile failutes.

To the Editor of the St. Croix þÿ Avis, Dear Sir, I take the liberty of sending you for publication some Extracts from the Assize Sermon of (he Bishop of Antigua, preached before the Governor, Chief Judge, and Grand Jury of that Island in the Cathedral on the 5th March last, which may he interesting, as having reference to the social condition of the Laboring Population of Antigua, as also containing some rental ks on the Island of St. Croix. This Sermon having been published by the request of those present, can be fully depended upon, so far as the Ext i acts go, as a lair and just estimate of the present social position of the class teferred to, in a Colony, where the principles of unlimited freedom were earliest developed, and most carefully fostered by the British Government. I am, your obdt. Servt. C. þÿ Whatever,also, may he said of the wisdom and the policy which in the first instance encouraged, if not compclh d, them to remove from the soil which they cultivated and to form the ¬ which now present, so marked a feature in our social arrangements, þÿ the effect of it, as a matter of fact, has been to isolate t lie labourer. It lias thus diminished the opportunities! of those kindly influences, on the part of employers or their repte.-entative , whivh tend so powerfully to hind society together and to exercise a beneficial and humanizing influence on the labouring pcor nn#*??#*#- Unspeakable as are the blessings of freedom, it has lost to the suljects ol it much of that attention to their comlerts and their wants

which was the only redeeming featuie in the system that has passed awrny. It is to be questioned whether that loss w u!d not have been lar less felt by them, had their houses on the estates been maintained in good repair, and their continued occupancy ol them at a lew leutal encouraged. As it is, the great majority, having acceded to the vill ges, have been thrown entirely upon their own resources and left to their own gnidmee. 1 have already intimated that their own true interests have been compromised, no less than the success of the Estates endangered by the absence of any means of inducing them to steady and continuous labour. Social evils have grown np among them, and are likely, unless arrested by benevolent effort, to be perpetuated. 1 will name hut one. VVheie they are located on Estates and under contract, the Liw seem cs to them medical attendance which in provided by the employer. Obviously no such gratuitous provision can follow tlnm into the Villages: and it would he harrowing to know how many a valuable life is sacrificed which might by timely care have been saved: while the quarterly returns of the R. gistiation Office tell a sad tale of the mortality amongst inlants. Thus, while we are debating the question if supplying the deficiency of labour by immigration from heathen land-, oui Christian population is, for want of due care, diminishing with a steadiness which no thoughtful or humane man can contemplate without a þÿshudder. þÿ Commonly, especially in the outlying villages,

the i ullages of the tabourets cousist but of one room rl lie herding together ol the sexes, arising out of this arrangement, even where it does not lead to actual immorality, is destructive of the deemey and modesty which are the safeguards of chastity. Tim condition of the cottages iu many cases is very unsatisfactory. No one unaccustomed to visit them promiscuously would easily believe the utter absence of all the appliances of domes tic comfort and civilivation which characterize some of these hovels. The actual wants of nature, in such a climate as this, are confined to food and shelter: and it there be natural indolence, the bousehol ler without a struggle resigns himself to the want of the commonest conveniences of life, except where he feels that he is the abject of remark. Hence our laboring poor are commonly well and od show days even gaily clad; bat the furniture at homo often consists of little more than the box which contains the Holiday suit. It must be confessed that the evil here i ndi eated is not peculiar to Antigua It is common

to the West India Islands. It prevails in many parts of advanced England. Hut ill ti e t er the evil does not remain uuuotued and uneaied for. All that philanthropy can do to abate and remedy it, is done. Iu no West India Colony, perhaps, are the laborers so comfortably domiciled as in the Danish Island of St. Croix There the laborer is invariably under annual contract , his dwelling being provided for him on the Estate. 'I he þÿlaborers houses ate under the inspection t f the Goverttnn nt, which is ttptaliy careful to provide lor them medical attendance in sickness, education for their children, and asylums lor the aged and infirm. l'l H-ibly some ot the provisions of the þÿ Labor þÿAct of that Island might be considered inconsistent with our notions ot Hiinsh freedom: f>r every adult person is required o $ have an occupation »nd to pursue it industi horsly. Hut there is no denying that a pnetmil care is exercised by the Government over the laboring class whose rights are jealously to guatd At any rate, they nowhere present the eye d. of the stranger such u picture of domestic comfort and healthiness as in that pic utestjun little þÿIsland.

The first thing which it would lie tlesirable to learn, in order to form a judgment as to the event, is the feeling in which the South has received these unusual demonstrations. The Northerners say that Mr. Jefferson Davis and Ins fellowtraitors are thoroughly frightened at the outburst ot Union patriotism. 1 h< y had, say the Unionists, no idea that the North was so indignant, and their doom so near. (From the New York Herald, May 18, 1861. ) The American War W8ws in Europe Paris, May 3, 1861. Since the receipt of the news from the United Slates, announcing that civil war had actu ally begun, the American troubles have become the principal topic of conversation in our jioiitieal circles, while the Paris and London journals are busily occupied with the same unfortunate subject. Americans shake hands with warmth, aud say, Thank God ! no blood was þÿshed; but they all feel how great a humiliation has fallen upon them, and they no longer boa-t so proudly of home government. We are twitted with the great failure that Ims overtaken us, and covert sneers are as plentiful as is a sympathy so expressed that wo cannot hut f. el how unreal it all is. I am assured by those whom I have ever found well inloinu d, that overtures have been made to this gove rnment by Spain, as regards the taking possession of the West India Islands. It was France that awoke Spain to the idea of conquest a short time back Napoleou III þÿ s advice caused her to uudertake the war with Morocco. With success grew the desire for more conquest, and so Spain seized upou the opportunity to annex the Dominic ins An angry protest from the Cabinet of the Tuilerics to that o! Madrid was met with all kinds of offeis

of division of spoils, and now Frauce thinks seriously of Hayti. South America will soon resound, I fear, to the bugles of France and the tricolor; aud þÿSpain yellow s and red standard will final where they never would have been raised had it not been for the intestine troubles ot the gieat republic. You, who are so busy with the uear approaches of that worst of all calamities, civil war, have not as yet time for sorrow. We in our auxiety and grief, are daily brought face to face with the fact that the prestige of the American nation is fading, and that already the uations of Europe are prepaiing to laud as masters in the New World. Dut a few months hack they would scarcely have dared to thiuk of that which now they are prepared to do. England speaks of her claim upoD Mexico, and here and iu London measuies are op nly discussed that are baaed upon a feeling that the United States are uow almost þÿpowerless May we not hope that these facts will awaken the American publio to the danger they run, and that, rising in their might, tbey may scatter to the winds the ambitious schemes of France, Spain and Eng and ? I am told that the turn affairs have taken in tbe United States will most likely put quite a new face on European matters. All is uow for peace, and it is even surmised that the great naval preparations made by France so lately, and that are going on now, will be turn, d to account iu the New World. I know from positive sources that the Emperor now desires peace at all bazad. He has

despatched agents to Russia, Austria, Rome and Sardinia, all charged wi h bringing ab<ut, if possible, a peaceful sol u' ion. Where France was before intriguing for war she now strives for peace. So it has been decided that the þÿF reuchtroops are to remain in Rome, and even that, if needs must, they will evacnate Syria. Tbe latter, however, will not be done unless it is impossible to procure England's coopcratiou with France in her views for aggrandizement in the New World, without a total giving up of þÿNapoleon s ambitious views as regards Turkey. The Wonderful Oil Springs of Pennsylvania. Oil springs have for a long tirrn been known to exist in the western part of Pennsylvania; hut when, a few months since, the fact was announced that a well had been opened from which good burning oil could he pumped in apparently inexhaustible quantities, many smiled incredulously, while others gave the item a turn or two in the mind, and then passed it as of little consequence. Having recently visited a portion of the oil regions, we drop it few observations. Titusville þÿ where the first well was opened þÿ is in Crawford county, Pa., | situated on Oil Creek, about forty miles southeast of Erie, and within about twenty-four hours ride of New York. The pioneer well was opened by Mr E. L. Drake in the fall of 1859. lie sunk a shaft 4£ inches in diameter through 29 feet of ear h and 30 feel ot rock. The result was, that instead of a daily yield of from 12 to 15 gallons as obtained front the spring, he struck a vein or crevice from which he readily pumped front 25 to 30 barrels per day. From the date of this discovery the excitement commenced. It was at once concluded that þÿDrake success s was an indication that under all that region was one vast lake of oil, and that all a man had to do was to bore his hole, and he would have a source of wealth more | sure and valuable than a gold mine. The more sanguine owners ol lands resolved not to sell at any price, although they could readily have taken at for which farms five times the amount their they previously held them offers dazzled by the tempting ; while a few, which so

much exceeded all former hopes, exchanged their lands for gold. Those who were the owners of the bottom lands leased out small portions of them on condition that the tenant should bore for oil, and, if successful, should pay as rent from one-third to one-half of all he might obtain. Many took leases of this kind, and were more or less successful ; while others, after spending their money and their efforts in vain, were compelled to give up for the want of means, yet fullv believing that if they could have gone a little deeper, their fortune would have turned. Indeed, there iR no limit to the poor þÿdriller hopes s hut his pocket, as oil has been found at all depths, from 70 feet to 500. Most of the oil is obtained by pumping, and a steam-engine is required for every pump. Large quantities of salt water are usually raised with the oil and discharged into a large vat ; the water runs out at a hole in the bottom, the oil runs off into a smaller vat through another orifice at the top, and from thence is drawn directly into barrels. The appearance of this oil in the crude state is as thin as water, and of a reddishbrown color. When it first comes from the wells it is as inflammable as spirit gas. Indeed, the gas often takes fire at the wells. Vats, derricks, barrels, and all have often been burned up by the careless use of a candle or match about the wells. In the process of distillation or refining, the crude oil parts with from 20 to 40 percent, of its original elements,
and becomes as pure and limpid as water, and as free from the explosive elements as whale oil. þÿ New York Independent, Feb. 7.

Although we need not fear that the Couueil will succeed in gaiuing the appioval of either the Government here or at home for their reekless scheme, still we think it is time there should be an end to such disgraceful doings, earned on year after year with the most barefaced impudence. For who ever heard in a civilized country, of the guardians and trustees of the commnmil funds sitting in conclave and voting the partition of these funds among themselves? How can the votes of those members count, who want the money for themselves? or of that member of the Council who wants the contract for the meal, to he proem ed by these funds? All these quorrit ft and surmises came near the truth, for we do think that Mr. A. speculated on all these objects simultaneously ; but Iris principal idea with the letter, ami especially with its publication, was most probably to create the effect which actually followed, namely to annihilate the credit of all other planters in the Island, so as to force them to embrace his scheme for getting anew advances from the Landtreasury. We have heard that many remarks have been made on the severity of the article, signed þÿ I>, which appeared in our last, and that some blame seems to lie imputed to us Grits insertion. A little reflection on the put of tlmse who are ever ready to blame, would p- rhaps convince them, that, if this paper is open for the expression of opinions, all that can he expected of us is impartiality towards our correspondents. As long as there exists a regularly appointed censor of the Press, the responsibility of an editor to the Public becomes less than if he alone were left to judge of the suitableness or tone of a communication. So long, therefore, ns the Censorship exists, wo deny the right of any one to attach blame to us for the publication of any article The censor stands between us and the public ; and we

think the object of that censorship has ever been to determine what is suitable or otherwise for publication. We therefore do not Icel ourselves called upon to assume other responsibilities than those which we already may have.

From the London Times , April 29. The challenge of the Confederate Stales has heen promptly accepted, and we can no longer object to 'resident Lincoln that he is without a designated policy. It we are to put a literal interpretation upon the document now before us, the Federal Government at Washington proclaims war, and calls | Major Anderson another to fight under; for an army of 73, 090 men. It' we are to accept the first impression created by President Lincoln's proclamation, the smoking out or binning out of Major Anderson is to he instantly resented by an invasion. What the President would not attempt to avert, what the fleet in the offlng would make no effort to oppose, anil what has heen so unaccountably accomplished without the loss of a single life, i\lr. Lincoln is determined to punish. In a State paper, so weak and wordy as to contrast strangely with those great historical documents which marked the birth of the American na- "I ion, the President denounces the þÿ "'combinations" existing in the seven insurgent States, si n d appeals to his fellowcitizens to "favour, facilitate, and aid" his efforts to maintain the Union and redress the wrongs of the North, (hilling lor 73,0 H) men, he indicates that his first object will tie to recover the Federal property, or, in other words, to fight his way to Charleston and there reinstate Major Anderson in his tort, the case-males of which are still in excellent order and the guns in serviceable condition. lie summons the Congress to meet at Washington on the 4th July,

Fort Sumter an " extraordinary occa- because he recognizes in the capture of sion" within the meaning of the text of the Constitution. He has taken his course promptly, and his decision is for war. IS ut is it quite certain that this document means exactly what it purports upon the surface to declare? Although it is as much a declaration of war as a President of the United Slates can issue, is it a declaration to tie followed up by instant war? Mav we not believe that, having made public declaration of a warlike policy, lie is inclined to follow it out in a deliberate and leisurely manner? May we not draw some inference from the fact that he has named no day for the rendezvous of the contingents of tl e Federal States, and that lie has named a distant day for the meeting of the Congress? Less than this proclamation President Lincoln could not have done. Of course, he could not surrender. If he had been prepared to let the South go lie would scarcely have acted so absurdly as to keep Major Anderson in an untenable fort, tempting an act of overt treason. The circumstance which he must have foreseen having taken place, it was necessary that he should take formal note of it, and mark it as an act of war. This lie has done. Ilut we will not even yet believe that these proclamations and these popular excitements actually mean real savage slaughter. It is not because the South Carolinians burnt the woodwork of a fort and smoked out the garrison that they are therefore, as some accounts say, " crazy

for a fight," and eager for the blood of their brethren of the North. It is not because President Lincoln has called for his 73,0(10 men that he is about to send them at once to engage in desperate and savage civil conflict. At present there seenis to he no great exasperation on either side. All the proceed-

S T þÿ c R 0 I X A\ Y Ij $ ings at Charleston have hitherto been carried on much as a cricket-match or an eight-oar race might take place in this country. The highest courtesy seems to have obtained on both sides. The ladies turn out to grace the contest. A good shot from Fort Sampler is as much applauded as a good shot front Fort to do with his 75,000 men when he has Moultrie. When the American flag is shot away General Beauregard sends

when the fori is found to be on fire the polite enemy, who has with such intense energy laboured to excite the conflagration, offers an equally energetic assistance to put it out. When the dispossessed enemv passes through the streets of Charleston the cheering of the people is frantic. The only indignation felt throughout the affair has been at the conduct of the American flotilla, which kept outside, and did not come into the harbour and take part in the fray. The Southerners resent this as an act of treachery towards their favourite enemv, Major Anderson. The courtesies, indeed, have been more fatal than the hostilities, for, whereas no life was destroyed hv the guns fired in anger, two men were killed and four wounded by the peaceful salute. Altogether, nothing can he more free front the ferocious hatreds which are distinctive of civil warfare than this bloodless Conflict has hitherto heen. Up to this time there is nothing in the conduct of the combatants to shut out hope of a peaceful solution of the difficulty. A moment, bowever, might change everything. At present Americans are shaking hands with each other all over the Union, and thanking God that no blood lias yet been spilt ; but if the Southerners should execute t heir threat of seizing Washington þÿ and, notwithstanding the promise of Pennsylvania to concentrate 100,001) men in the city in 48 hours, (lie design seems by no means impracticable, þÿ then we shall have war in earnest. Or, if Mr. Lincoln should send his Militia to

force a way through the frontier States, and a battle should be fought ; or if he should attempt to land an army on the shores of South Carolina ; or if the States upon the upper bank of the Mississippi should excite to insurrection the black population of the States that lie upon the lower bank of that river, then we fear that we shall see civil war in all its horrors, and we shall abandon all trust in the good sense of our Transatlantic kinsman. But the present news does not seem by any means to go this length. It may, indeed, mean all that we in F.ngland, who have been so proud of our strong blustering son, most dread, and a few more weeks may show lis Anglo-Saxons rushing at each others' throats. But it may also mean that the President is only taking his formal position, consequent upon the act of hostility committed by the South, and that he still intends to carry out a policy of procrastination. It is by no means certain that a state of armed preparation is not a necessary condition to the settlement of this question even if its solution is to lie peaceful. The parties are not now in presence of each other. No great momentary peril impends. It is only little acts of hostility which have as yet been committed. Just at first these may be inflicted and endured with good humour, but that temper would soon change under frequent provocation, and the two parties are much more likely to smoulder into a state of fiery exasperation if they are constantly engaged in little conflicts

than if they are only prepared for a great fight. Willi hostile armies in the field, each learns to measure and to respect his enemy; with real preparation for war comes a knowledge of the difficulties as well as of the dangers of such a war. What is President Lincoln

got them together? We grant that lie has the wealth of the nation to back him, that he has the most undivided population, that þÿ the better cause although a democracy he has, if' you please, has no bond of loyalty such as that we own, and no sense of honour or fealty to a Sovereign Power; but, granting all this, what is President Lincoln to do with his 75 OHO men ? lie has ships, but not ships enough to transport this army to the harbour of Charleston. He has money, but not money enough to maintain this army in an enemy's country. How is he to get to this Fort Sumtert Is he to march his army across the Border States? Does he propose to obtain a free march across Virginia, or to force his way if a free passage should be refused? When this formidable difficulty is surmounted, does he expect with 75,900 men to traverse North Carolina, and to pass through the whole length of South Carolina? We did not find it so easy to march regular troops through America even when its defenders were far less numerous than they now are. The idea of a laud invasion with any detachment he could spare from his 75,000 men is evidently impossible. A descent by sea is hardly less out of the question in the face of an armed population and considering the limited force of the States' navy. How, then, is Mr. Lincoln to get to Fort Sumter? We can hardly think that he is serious when he so coolly says that " the first service "assigned " be to repossess the forts." No to the forces will probably doubt,

there is much that he might do. He might set fire to the four corners of the new Republic. He might land a force and excite a servile war in the Gulf States ; he might penetrate those States by the line of the Mississippi ; he might create Republics of free blacks all along the north of the Gulf of Mexico. Those slaves for which the South are fighting are their weakness in the contest as well as their incentive to the contest. But we can hardly think that the North is prepared for such extreme measures as this, or that a massacre of whites and a great territory possessed by independent blacks could suit the views of any American statesman. May we not rather hope that this preparation for war may turn out to be a preparation for negotiating, and the preliminary steps either to reunion, or at least to peace? We may doubtless he in some measure biassed by our own obvious interests in thus balancing the chances of immediate civil war; for so nearly are our interests intertwined with America that civil war in the States means destitution in Lancashire. But still we think it reasonable to hope that this proclamation is not the " word" which immediately precedes the " blow," and that even if the Americans should ultimately he so foolish as to fight among themselves we may yet have a little time to guard ourselves from the consequences which any such event would at this moment entail upon our own population.

(London Times, July 2, 1861 ) A Steamer Descending Niagara RlVER þÿ A correspondent of the Courier writes from iagartt Falls, under date of June 7 : þÿ þÿ The monotony of life at Niagara Falls was broken today by an episode. It was rumoured lliat the little steamer Maid of the Mist was about to attempt an exploit. Report said that Mr. Buchanan had sold her to

parties on Lake Ontario, to be delivered on that tranquil sheet of water, and that at least one individual in your city bad a lien on her which would be seriously invalidated in case the Maid should succeed in finding anchorage at a British dock. It was said, moreover, that said individual was making quick time hitherward to prevent the absquatulation of his property ; but the idea that anything made of wood could outlive a voyage down these terrific rapids Was regarded as absurd. The prospect of its being tried, however, drew at least 30(1 or 400 people to the hanks ot the river. All day there had been a bustle of mysterious preparation on hoard the steamer. Hatches were being nailed down anil everything made taut, hut no satisfaction could be had by inquiring minds. A little past 3 she cut loose from her moorings about a quarter of tr mile above the bridge, and steamed gallantly up towards the Falls. A murmur of disappointed expectation ran through the crowd, when suddenly, as she reach ed a point about half way up to the Falls, she turned with a graceful curve and headed downwards. There were on board Iter engineer, Robinson, famed for deeds of daring in these parts, and, I believe, three others. The Maid came down with current, and hung, quivering, hut otherwise motionless, just opposite Iter dork. Il seemed its if the daughter of the spray were undecided. The moments were long before she made up her mind. In an instant, before a spectator could wink, the die was cast, and she

puffed a farewell to her home under the cliffs. Another second, and she swung in the sinewy grasp of' the mighty river, speeding like an arrow down the stream. There was a rush of excited beholders for the bridge, and looking up thence it was a brave and thrilling sight to see her coming down and dipping like a water-fowl under the spray. Your readers know how Niagara looks just under and just below the bridge. The giant offspring of four lakes writhes there like ti chained monster. The water, where it is not a mass of angry foam, proceeded to cede the islands, which ' seems as hard as iron, and wears a hue of sickly green, ominous, voracious, deadly. There is the force of an angry ocean pent between these narrow prison walls, as the water, tortured into foam, dashes down the staircase of rocks. No one thought she could live through it. but after the first moment of hesitation Magistrate, Mr. Moir. proceeded in II. j Niagara had been her father. As rite she leaped into the gorge as though passed under the bridge the crowd rushed to the other side and trembled for the safety of the (hiring crew, for the critical point was yet to be reached. Again and again she shol overhead in foam, and again and again, as site all but disappeared, it was thought that the river had claimed its own. But the Maid w s native to the cataract and bore a charmed life. With one blow of a seething breaker her smoke-stack was levelled with the deck, and then every body gave her up. At hist she had run

the terrible gauntlet, and emerged dripping and quivering upon the calm water of the whirlpool. That Charyhdis was easy after the Scylla she had weathered. A wide sweep with the current, and she Buffalo was lost to sight. She belongs to Ontario now, and Iter creditors may follow, if they dare.
